To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the character of biological workloads differs significantly from that of multimedia workloads, and thus different optimization heurists are needed.

the character of biological data is different from that of multimedia data, and that this difference is reflected in the performance of the indexing structures and the heuristics that are used for them.

(1) for biological similarity search, the most widely used indexing structures are not optimal; (2) a pivot selection heuristic that is sensitive to the actual distribution of data is better than the most widely used heuristic for corner selection; (3) data partitioning that is sensitive to data distribution is better than the widely used median split heuristic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a theoretical and experimental understanding of the properties of biological workloads, and the implications for indexing.
developing new techniques for optimizing the performance of distance-based indexing for biological applications.
developing new heuristics for similarity search in biological databases, and we believe that these heuristics will be applicable to other distance-based similarity search applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
distance-based index structures are not a panacea for biological similarity search problems.
for biological applications, it is better to use a pivot selection heuristic that finds centers rather than corner selection heuristics.

the biological data types we consider here are not intrinsicaly high dimensional, and the heuristics that are most effective for multimedia applications are not necessarily the best choice for biological data types.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a new distance-based indexing approach for biological databases that outperforms state-of-the-art indexing approaches by 2-3x on real data.
the biological similarity search problem is different from its multimedia counterpart, and that we have developed a number of new techniques that can be used to improve performance.
the character of biological similarity search workloads is different enough to warrant different optimizations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the biological similarity search problem is sufficiently different from multimedia similarity search that it deserves a different set of optimization strategies.
biological workloads are sufficiently different from multimedia work loads, that the optimization heuristics developed for one are not necessarily optimal for the other.
the character of biological data is different from multimedia and other workloads, and thus, different optimization techniques are needed.
